purpose: Provide the basis of preparation and “how to read this report” gateway for sustainability-related financial disclosures. Establish compliance posture, reporting scope and boundaries, qualitative characteristics, connected information principles, comparability approach, and the relationship to the broader corporate reporting suite.
tone: Formal, standards-aligned, and compliance-oriented. Use assurance-like phrasing that emphasizes fair presentation, completeness, neutrality, accuracy, and absence of material error. Maintain balanced transparency by acknowledging limitations, estimation uncertainty, and evolving reporting maturity. Treat forward-looking information cautiously by stating assumptions and judgement basis. Use reader-guidance language to explain where the disclosures sit within the overall reporting package.
level_of_detail: High-level but specific enough to be auditable: define scope, boundaries, standards applied, and key preparation principles; describe methodologies (e.g., materiality process) as steps and inputs rather than outcomes. Defer detailed results, entity lists, and granular indices to appendices or referenced sections.
paragraph_style: Start with a short declarative opener (reporting scope/timeframe and compliance statement). Follow with compact paragraphs and bullet lists for principles and methodologies. Use clear subsection headers with brief intent-setting lead sentences. Close with cross-references/signposts to where detailed supporting information can be found.
sentence_style: Short-to-medium length, precise, and unambiguous. Prefer active voice for responsibilities and determinations (e.g., “management determined…”), and neutral/passive voice where appropriate for standards framing (e.g., “disclosures are prepared in accordance with…”). Use defined terms consistently and avoid marketing language.
preferred_evidence_style: Substantiate preparation approach by referencing applicable standards and internal reporting boundaries/policies. Evidence should be process-based (steps taken, inputs used, governance linkages) and traceability-based (cross-references to financial statements, appendices, indices). Clearly distinguish current-period disclosures from contextual comparative references.
table_usage: Use simple, low-density tables only where they improve traceability or scanability (e.g., mapping of requirement themes to disclosure locations; applicability mapping of industry/sector guidance to business activities; stakeholder grouping). Keep tables descriptive and avoid performance claims.
figure_usage: Use minimal, schematic visuals to clarify boundaries and methodology (e.g., reporting boundary/value chain schematic; stakeholder grouping panels; materiality process flow). Include a short caption that explains what the reader is viewing and why it matters.
how_to_discuss_missing_data: State transparently when information is unavailable, incomplete, or subject to estimation uncertainty. Explain the reason (e.g., data limitations, system maturity, methodological constraints), the approach used (e.g., estimates, proxies, controls), and the plan to improve (e.g., strengthening processes, controls, and coverage) without overpromising timelines or outcomes. Clearly label any comparative limitations.
what_to_avoid: Jurisdiction-specific legal or regulatory assertions that may not apply
Specific dates, reporting-year identifiers, or period-specific claims
Currency references or presentation currency choices
Entity-specific incorporation history, merger history, or statutory citations
Lists of subsidiaries, branch counts, ownership percentages, or location inventories
Named business segment labels or acronyms unique to a particular organization
Claims of achievements, awards, endorsements, or performance outcomes in this section
Exact note/appendix numbering or cross-reference identifiers from any reference report
Overly definitive forward-looking statements without stating assumptions and uncertainty
Duplicating detailed topical disclosures that belong in later sections
